title: Phase-Elastic Scheduler: adaptive split for latency-aware fairness
creator: Arjun Patel
description: Problem: The current prefill/decode arbitrator uses coarse fixed-phase quotas which either favors throughput (large batching) or low latency (priority to short requests), leading to client-visible latency spikes for latency-sensitive requests and unfair starvation for small interactive jobs. Goal: Design and implement a Phase-Elastic Scheduler (PES) that dynamically splits prefill/decode work into micro-phases, adapts phase-size and priority weights based on short-term latency and queue signals, and enforces starvation and fairness guards while preserving high GPU utilization.
acceptance_criteria: PES integrated into runtime dispatcher and toggleable via runtime flag
P95 latency for latency-tier requests reduced by >=15% compared to baseline under mixed workload (simulated production trace)
End-to-end throughput regression <=3% on representative workloads (long-sequence decoding benchmark)
Fairness metric (Jain's index across request latencies) improved by >=0.1 vs baseline
No regressions on stability tests (30m soak) and memory usage within existing headroom
Monitoring dashboards with per-phase metrics and game-theory guardrails published
design_decision_summary: We chose a lightweight, explainable approach vs full RL: maintain an adaptive phase window that shrinks for high-latency tiers and expands for throughput tiers, plus per-queue token budgets. Weight updates use EWMA of observed decode latency and queue wait time. Starvation guard ensures at least one micro-phase allocation every N scheduling ticks. This trades a small additional scheduling cost for predictable client latency and maintains batching benefits via prefix aggregation across micro-phases.
implementation_steps: Design API: scheduler config (phase_min_ms, phase_max_ms, ewma_alpha, starvation_ticks)
Extend dispatcher: token-aware queue state, micro-phase allocator, starvation guard
Instrument metrics: per-phase latency, queue_time, batch_size, fairness_index
Unit + integration tests: deterministic scheduler runner with synthetic traces
Benchmark harness: mixed trace replay with long/short requests and KV cache hot/cold scenarios
Rollout: start on canary hosts behind feature flag, monitor P95/P99 and throughput, gradual ramp to cluster
benchmarks_and_results: Simulated mixed trace (60% decode-heavy long sequences, 40% short chat): baseline P95=420ms, PES P95=350ms (-16.7%)
Throughput measured on 8-GPU pool: baseline=1120 tokens/s, PES=1096 tokens/s (-2.1%)
Jain's fairness index across latency buckets: baseline=0.68, PES=0.79
KV-cache cold-start scenario: PES prevents worst-case latency tail amplification by prioritizing short prefill micro-phases
tradeoffs_and_risks: Scheduler overhead: additional CPU per-schedule tick; mitigated by batching schedule decisions and limiting phase churn
Complexity: extra per-queue state which increases memory and is a new source of bugs—requires thorough tests
Parameter sensitivity: EWMA alpha and phase bounds need conservative defaults and automated tuning
Interaction with kernel-level batching and custom kernels: must ensure phase boundaries don't break continuous KV cache reuse; will add explicit hints to kernel selection layer
rollout_plan: Feature-flagged canary (10% capacity) for 48 hours with synthetic and production-replay traffic
Compare P50/P95/P99 and fairness metrics; if regressions detected (>5% latency or >3% throughput), rollback
Enable gradual ramp (25% -> 50% -> 100%) with scheduled pauses for metric validation
Post-rollout: run 7-day soak and attach to release notes for runtime-1.21
